flat.title: My new flat
flat.text:
Hi Mum!

I'm in my new flat in Manchester. It's small, but it's really nice. There are three rooms: a living room, a bedroom and a kitchen. There's a bathroom too, of course, with a shower. There isn't a bath.

The living room is my favourite room. There's a big blue sofa and there are two chairs. The TV is opposite the sofa. There's a table next to the window, and my laptop is on the table. There are some shelves above the table, but there aren't any books on them — the books are still in boxes under my bed!

In the bedroom there's a bed, a wardrobe and a small desk. There's a mirror on the wall between the wardrobe and the door.

The kitchen is very small. There's a fridge and a cooker, but there isn't a table. There's a balcony, and there are some plants on it. There isn't a garden.

Are there any shops near the flat? Yes, there are! There's a supermarket opposite the house.

Love,
Emma

day.title: A day in my life
day.text:
My name's Sarah and I'm a nurse. I work at a hospital in Leeds. My day starts very early!

I get up at half past five. I have a shower, get dressed and have breakfast. I usually have coffee and toast. I never eat a big breakfast. I leave home at quarter past six and I take the bus to work. I don't drive because I haven't got a car.

I start work at seven o'clock. I work from seven to three. We don't have a long lunch break: I have lunch at about twelve, and I usually eat in the hospital café. In the afternoon I'm always tired.

I finish work at three o'clock and I go home. My daughter Lily finishes school at half past three, so I'm at home before her. In the evening I cook dinner and we eat at six. After dinner Lily does her homework and I do the housework. Then I sometimes watch TV with my husband, but I often go to bed at nine!

I don't work on Saturdays and Sundays. At the weekend I get up late, at eight o'clock.

week.text:
Jack: Mum says you study in the evening, Emma. Is that true?
Emma: Yes, it is. I work in an office from nine to five, and then I go to university on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
Jack: What time do you get home?
Emma: At about ten. I'm always tired on Wednesday mornings!
Jack: Do you study at the weekend too?
Emma: I usually study on Sunday afternoons. On Saturdays I never study. I go to the gym in the morning and I meet friends in the evening.
Jack: Does Dan go to the gym with you?
Emma: No, he doesn't. He hates the gym! He plays football twice a week. What about you? What do you do after school?
Jack: I do my homework first. Then I play computer games.
Emma: Every day?
Jack: No! Mum doesn't like it. Only on Fridays and at the weekend.

club.title: The weekend club
club.text:
Welcome to the Leeds Weekend Club! We're a group of people who love doing things together in our free time.

On Saturday mornings we go running in the park. You don't need to be fast — we run slowly and we talk a lot! After that we usually have coffee together.

On Saturday afternoons there's a chess club in the library. Can you play chess? It doesn't matter if you can't. Tom can teach you. He's very good at it and he's a great teacher.

On Sundays we often go walking or cycling outside the city. We also go swimming once a month. If it rains, we stay in and play cards or watch a film.

Are you interested in music? Some of us play the guitar and sing. We aren't very good, but it's a lot of fun.

You can join us for one activity or for all of them. It's free, and you can bring your friends. Write to us or call Emma — she can tell you more.

town.title: My town
town.text:
I live in a small town called Ashford. It's about sixty kilometres from London. It takes forty minutes by train.

The town centre is very nice. In the middle of the town there's a big square with a market every Saturday. There's an old church on one side of the square and a library on the other side. The post office is on the corner of the square and High Street. Next to it there's a bakery — they sell delicious bread.

High Street is the main street. There are a lot of shops, two banks, a chemist's and three cafés. At the end of High Street there's a bridge over the river. If you go across the bridge and turn right, you get to the park. I walk through the park every morning on my way to work.

I usually go to work on foot because my office is near my house. It only takes fifteen minutes. But when it rains, I go by bus. The bus stop is opposite my house. I get on there and get off at the third stop.

There isn't a cinema or a shopping centre in Ashford, so at the weekend we often go to London.

year.title: The weather where I live
year.text:
I live in Edinburgh, in Scotland. People say the weather here is terrible, but I don't agree. It's just… interesting.

In winter it's cold and dark. It gets dark at four o'clock in the afternoon! It sometimes snows in January and February, but not much. I always wear a warm coat, a scarf and gloves.

Spring starts in March. It's still cool, but the days are longer and there are flowers in the parks. It often rains in April, so I never leave home without an umbrella.

Summer is my favourite season. It isn't hot — usually about eighteen degrees — but in June it's light until eleven o'clock at night. In August there's a big festival and the city is full of people.

In autumn the trees are red and yellow. It's very windy in October and November, and it rains a lot.

Right now it's November. I'm sitting at my window and looking at the street. It's raining, the wind is blowing and people are running for the bus. But I'm drinking hot tea and I'm warm and dry.

weekend.title: A terrible Saturday
weekend.text:
Last Saturday was the worst day of my year.

I wanted to go to London for my friend Anna's birthday party. I woke up late because I forgot to set my alarm. I didn't have time for breakfast. I ran to the station, but I missed my train by one minute!

The next train was an hour later. I bought a coffee and sat on the platform. It was cold and it started to rain. Then I looked in my bag for Anna's present — and it wasn't there. It was at home, on the kitchen table.

I finally arrived in London at two o'clock. I took the underground, but I got on the wrong train and went north, not south. I lost another forty minutes.

When I got to Anna's flat, the door was closed and nobody answered. I called her. “Where are you?” she asked. “At your flat!” I said. She laughed. “Tom, the party is next Saturday!”

In the end we went to a café and had a wonderful afternoon. And the next week I didn't forget the present.

life.title: My grandmother
life.text:
My grandmother's name was Helen. She was born in 1935 in a small village in Scotland. Her family wasn't rich. There were six children, and they all lived in a house with two bedrooms.

She left school when she was fourteen and started work in a shop. She didn't like it, but she needed the money. In the evenings she studied, because she wanted to be a nurse.

In 1955 she moved to Edinburgh and got a job at a hospital. She met my grandfather there. He was a patient — he had a broken leg! They got married in 1958 and had three children.

My grandmother worked as a nurse for forty years. She never drove a car and she never flew in a plane. But she read hundreds of books and she could speak French, because she learned it from the radio.

When I was a child, I stayed with her every summer. She made wonderful cakes and told me stories about the past. She died ten years ago, and I still think about her every day.

plans.title: Next year
plans.text:
Emma: Dan, it's almost the end of the year. What are your plans for next year?
Dan: Well, first, I'm going to change jobs. I don't like my office. It's too far from home and my boss is the worst manager in the company.
Emma: Really? What are you going to do?
Dan: I'm going to look for a job in a smaller company. Smaller companies are friendlier, I think. And I'd like to work nearer home.
Emma: Good idea. I'm going to finish my course in June. Then I'm going to take the exam.
Dan: Are you going to pass?
Emma: I hope so! I'm going to study every evening. It's the most difficult exam of the course.
Dan: And what about the summer? Are we going to go to Barcelona again?
Emma: I'd like to go to a different place this time. What about Scotland? It's cheaper than Spain, and it's more beautiful.
Dan: But it's colder! And it's going to rain every day.
Emma: Maybe. But the mountains are wonderful. And my grandmother's village is there.
Dan: OK, Scotland in July. But I'm going to take a very warm jumper.

cities.title: Three cities
cities.text:
People often ask me: which is the best city in the UK? I lived in three of them, so here is my answer.

London is the biggest and the most famous. About nine million people live there. It's also the most expensive: a small flat costs more than a big house in the north. London is noisier and busier than other cities, but it's the most interesting place for museums, theatres and food from all over the world.

Manchester is smaller and cheaper than London. It's the best city for music and football. The people are friendlier, I think, and life is slower. But the weather is worse — it rains more than in London.

Edinburgh is the smallest of the three, and for me it's the most beautiful. It's older and quieter than Manchester, with a castle in the middle of the city. It's colder than London, and in winter the days are much shorter. But in summer it's as busy as London, because of the festival.

So which is the best? In my opinion, London is the best for a weekend, Manchester is the best for a night out, and Edinburgh is the best for life.
